crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: AI and Authorship
children.blurb: AI and authorship covers the questions of who or what counts as an author when a model contributes to a text, an image, a dataset or a piece of code, and how credit, accountability and originality are assigned in that arrangement.

children.name: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
children.blurb: Fabricated citations are references that look plausible but point to papers, authors, journals or DOIs that do not exist, or that misattribute real work to the wrong source.

children.name: Training Data and Academic Work
children.blurb: Training data in academic work covers the corpora, datasets and text collections that machine learning models learn from, together with the scholarly record those collections are drawn from.

children.name: Ethics Review with AI Assistance
children.blurb: Ethics review with AI assistance covers the use of machine learning tools inside institutional review boards, research ethics committees, and similar bodies that assess human subjects research, animal work, and dual use concerns.

children.name: Provenance of Research Images and Data
children.blurb: Provenance of research images and data covers the record of where a figure, dataset, or measurement came from, who handled it, and what was done to it before publication.

sections.body: Governance, ethics and research integrity covers the rules and habits that keep scholarly work honest when AI tools are part of the process. In practice this means deciding who counts as an author when a model helped draft or analyse, checking whether a cited paper actually exists, and tracing where training data came from. Researchers now use AI to summarise literature, suggest citations, draft sections and generate figures, and each of those uses creates a paper trail that has to be examined. The work is less about banning tools and more about making their contribution visible and verifiable. It sits at the meeting point of journal policy, institutional review and everyday lab practice.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are settled in principle but messy in practice. Most journals now say a model cannot be an author because it cannot take responsibility, yet disclosure rules vary and enforcement is uneven. Fabricated citations are a known failure mode, and checking them is largely manual, slow and easy to skip under deadline pressure. Training data provenance is often opaque, since many models do not disclose their sources, which makes it hard to confirm whether a dataset or text was used lawfully or ethically. Ethics review boards are still working out when an AI-assisted study needs full review and when it does not. The honest limit is that detection tools are unreliable, so verification depends on human checking rather than automated certainty.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the life of a research project from writing to review to publication. AI and Authorship deals with credit and responsibility, which is the first question a collaborator faces. Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking takes on the reference list, where invented sources do the most visible damage. Training Data and Academic Work looks upstream at where models get their material and what that means for scholarship. Ethics Review with AI Assistance covers the approval process and how boards should treat AI involvement. Provenance of Research Images and Data closes the loop by asking whether figures and datasets can be traced to their origin. A reader would go to the first for authorship disputes, the second for citation checking, the third for data sourcing, the fourth for review procedure and the fifth for image and data integrity.
